newsitem.title: USA: U.S. May output gain depicts lively manufacturing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. May output gain depicts lively manufacturing.

text.p: The U.S. May industrial production data released on Tuesday depicted the fourth consecutive monthly output gain since February and challenged the notion of an economy that is slowing to trend growth, economists said.

"The industrial production number was a good one for the economy," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "It suggests that the manufacturing sector is continuing to hold its own and is putting in a good performance in the second quarter."

The Federal Reserve reported that U.S. industrial output rose 0.4 percent in May. The Fed also reported that production rose 0.3 percent in April, contrary to the flat reading on output originally reported for the month. U.S. industrial output rose 0.4 percent in March and 0.5 percent in February.

Dana Johnson, managing director at First Chicago Capital Markets, said the recent pattern of "pretty strong" industrial production data "fits very nicely with a lot of other data on the manufacturing sector," including the new orders trend in the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) data and the low level of inventories relative to sales.
"All of these things suggest that the manufacturing sector is in really good shape," he said.
Johnson said the industrial production data go counter to the notion that the economy will slow to a non-inflationary growth trend.

"We've had a bit of a lull in consumer spending and that has created the impression that the economy may be downshifting and this number is a real challenge to that perception," said Johnson. "This (bond) market has gone too far in adopting the view that growth will slow to trend."
U.S. bond prices, which slipped on profit-taking after a May Consumer Price Index (CPI) report that was as benign as the market expected, deteriorated further after the industrial production report.

At 1010 EDT/1410 GMT, the 30-year bond was down 16/32 to 98-19/32, yielding 6.73 percent. Shortly before the industrial production/capacity utilization figures were released at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT, the benchmark 30-year bond was down 6/32.
Alan Ruskin, chief economist at I.D.E.A., said output data over the last four months are consistent with annualized manufacturing output growth of about five percent.
Ruskin said an annualized output growth rate of five percent would run "just a little bit ahead of productivity growth and is therefore creating modest gains in employment."

The Fed also reported that capacity utilization, the portion of the nation's mines, factories and utilities employed in the month's production, rose to 83.7 in May from 83.6 in April. The May level was the highest in more than one and a half years and "is high enough to leave Fed officials concerned about the level of resource utilization and inflation," said Moran.
But Moran said he did not expect the Fed to raise interest rates in July.

"The industrial production numbers are solid, but the CPI (Consumer Price Index) remains restrained," he said, referring to the Labor Department's report that the CPI rose just 0.1 percent in May. "Final demand appears as though it's slowing, so I think the Fed will be patient and wait."
